title: Subprocess jail for untrusted code
description: A subprocess jail runs untrusted archive code in a child process with no shell, a scrubbed environment, and captured I/O. The engine spawns the code via subprocess with shell=False, a minimal env, and pipes; the parent enforces timeouts and reads only bounded output. A misbehaving child cannot touch the parent's memory or files. Use it as the baseline isolation for running archive-submitted programs.
demo:
import subprocess, sys
code = "print(sum(range(10)))"
p = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", code], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10, env={})
print("jailed output:", p.stdout.strip(), "| return:", p.returncode)
assert p.stdout.strip() == "45" and p.returncode == 0

t: Filesystem jail with temp working directory
title: Filesystem jail with temp working directory
description: A filesystem jail confines untrusted code to a fresh temporary directory so it cannot read or write the host's files. The engine creates an empty temp dir, sets it as the child's working directory, and deletes it afterwards; path checks reject any '..' escapes. The archive's real files stay untouched. Use it when sandboxed programs need scratch file space.
demo:
import tempfile, os
jail = tempfile.mkdtemp()
p = os.path.join(jail, "note.txt")
open(p, "w").write("sandboxed")
print("jail contents:", os.listdir(jail))
assert os.listdir(jail) == ["note.txt"]
import shutil; shutil.rmtree(jail)
assert not os.path.exists(jail)

title: Privilege dropping for sandboxed workers
description: Privilege dropping sheds dangerous capabilities from the sandbox worker before untrusted code runs. On POSIX the engine can setuid to a 'nobody' user, clear supplementary groups, and apply a restrictive umask; on any platform it at minimum scrubs secrets from the environment. Less privilege means less damage from escape. Use it to minimize the blast radius if code escapes the jail.

t: CPU time limits with watchdog timeout
title: CPU time limits with watchdog timeout
description: CPU time limits kill sandboxed programs that run too long, enforced by a watchdog the untrusted code cannot disable. The engine runs the child with a hard timeout; on expiry it terminates, then kills the whole process tree after a grace period. Infinite loops become brief timeouts instead of hung workers. Use it on every untrusted execution without exception.
demo:
import subprocess, sys
code = "import time; time.sleep(30)"
try:
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", code], timeout=2, capture_output=True)
    outcome = "finished?!"
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    outcome = "watchdog killed it"
print(outcome)
assert outcome == "watchdog killed it"

title: Memory caps for sandboxed processes
description: Memory caps bound how much RAM a sandboxed program may allocate, enforced by the OS so the program cannot negotiate. The engine sets RLIMIT_AS / RLIMIT_DATA via the resource module (or cgroup limits in containers) before exec; allocations past the cap fail cleanly. Runaway allocations die instead of starving the host. Use it alongside CPU limits for complete resource bounding.
demo:
import resource
soft, hard = resource.getrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS)
print("address-space limit (bytes):", soft if soft > 0 else "unlimited")
resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS, (soft, hard))  # re-assert current
print("cap re-asserted without error: OK")

t: Output size caps on sandbox I/O
title: Output size caps on sandbox I/O
description: Output caps truncate or kill sandboxed programs that spew unbounded bytes, protecting logs and pipes. The engine reads child output incrementally and aborts past a byte budget; partial output is preserved up to the cap with a truncation note. Fork-bombs of print statements are contained. Use it to keep sandboxed output from flooding the archive system.
demo:
import subprocess, sys
code = "for i in range(100000): print('x'*100)"
p = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", code], capture_output=True, timeout=10)
capped = p.stdout[:1000]
print("captured then capped at:", len(capped), "bytes of", len(p.stdout))
assert len(capped) == 1000 < len(p.stdout)

title: Import whitelist for sandboxed code
description: An import whitelist lets sandboxed code use only approved modules, blocking os, socket, and other dangerous imports. The engine installs a meta-path finder that raises ImportError for anything not on the list; the whitelist covers safe stdlib (math, json, itertools) plus archive-approved helpers. Dangerous capability never loads. Use it to defang untrusted code at the import boundary.

title: AST scanning for dangerous calls
description: AST scanning statically rejects sandboxed code containing dangerous constructs before it ever runs. The engine parses the code and walks the syntax tree, rejecting names like eval, exec, open, __import__, and attribute access to dunders; rejection happens at submit time with a clear message. Static analysis complements runtime jails. Use it as a fast first gate before heavier sandboxing.
demo:
import ast
BANNED = {"eval", "exec", "open", "__import__", "compile"}
def scan(code):
    tree = ast.parse(code)
    bad = [n.id for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Name) and n.id in BANNED]
    return bad
print("scan('eval(x)'):", scan("eval(x)"), "| scan('1+1'):", scan("1+1"))
assert scan("eval(x)") == ["eval"] and scan("1+1") == []
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Restricted builtins for sandbox globals
description: Restricted builtins replace the sandbox's global namespace with a safe subset, removing file and process access. The engine exec's untrusted code with __builtins__ limited to harmless functions (len, range, sum, print); anything else raises NameError. Even if code runs, it has no tools for mischief. Use it for lightweight in-process sandboxing of simple snippets.
demo:
safe = {"__builtins__": {"len": len, "range": range, "sum": sum}}
ns = {}
exec("total = sum(range(5))", safe, ns)
print("computed:", ns["total"])
try: exec("open('x')", safe, {}); escaped = True
except NameError: escaped = False
print("open blocked:", not escaped)
assert ns["total"] == 10 and not escaped
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Network isolation for sandboxed code
description: Network isolation denies sandboxed code all socket access so untrusted programs cannot exfiltrate data or attack others. The engine blocks the socket module (import gate or firewall rules) and runs with no network namespace in containers; DNS and HTTP both fail fast. Data can only leave through the engine's controlled output channel. Use it for any sandbox handling sensitive archive data.
demo:
import socket
real = socket.socket
class Dead:
    def __init__(self, *a, **k): raise OSError("network isolated")
socket.socket = Dead
try: socket.socket(); leaked = True
except OSError: leaked = False
socket.socket = real
print("socket blocked:", not leaked)
assert not leaked

title: Stdout and stderr capture
description: Output capture routes a sandboxed program's stdout and stderr into bounded buffers the engine controls. The engine swaps sys.stdout/sys.stderr (in-process) or pipes (subprocess) and reads with size caps; captured text becomes part of the execution result record. Nothing prints to the host's console unmediated. Use it to collect and bound all sandboxed program output.
demo:
import io, contextlib
buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
    print("hello from sandbox")
out = buf.getvalue()
print("captured:", out.strip())
assert out.strip() == "hello from sandbox"

title: Input size validation before execution
description: Input validation rejects oversized or malformed sandbox submissions before they consume any resources. The engine checks code length, input data size, and argument counts against configured maxima; rejections are instant and logged. It stops resource attacks at the front door. Use it as the cheapest sandbox defense.
demo:
MAX_CODE, MAX_INPUT = 10000, 1000000
def admit(code, data):
    if len(code) > MAX_CODE: return "code too large"
    if len(data) > MAX_INPUT: return "input too large"
    return "admitted"
print(admit("x=1", "d"), "|", admit("x"*20000, "d"))
assert admit("x=1", "d") == "admitted" and admit("x"*20000, "d") == "code too large"
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Deterministic seed injection
description: Seed injection fixes all randomness in sandboxed runs so results reproduce bit-for-bit. The engine seeds Python's random, numpy, and hash randomization (PYTHONHASHSEED) before execution and records the seed in the result. Identical code plus identical seed always yields identical output. Use it to make sandboxed archive experiments reproducible.
demo:
import random
def run(seed):
    random.seed(seed)
    return [random.random() for _ in range(3)]
a, b = run(7), run(7)
print("reproducible:", a == b)
assert a == b and run(8) != a

title: Frozen environment recording
description: Environment recording snapshots the sandbox's software versions with each run so results stay interpretable forever. The engine records interpreter version, library versions, and OS details into the result record; replays pin the same versions. 'Works on my machine' becomes checkable history. Use it for audit-grade reproducibility of sandboxed runs.
demo:
import sys, platform
env = {"python": sys.version.split()[0], "os": platform.system()}
print("frozen env:", env)
assert env["python"].count(".") == 2

title: Result hashing for execution integrity
description: Result hashing fingerprints every sandbox execution's outputs so tampering or nondeterminism is detectable. The engine hashes stdout, return code, and result files with SHA-256 into the execution record; re-running and comparing hashes proves integrity. Mismatches flag nondeterminism or interference. Use it to verify sandboxed results haven't been altered.
demo:
import hashlib
def fingerprint(stdout, code):
    return hashlib.sha256(f"{code}:{stdout}".encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
f1 = fingerprint("45\n", 0)
print("fingerprint:", f1)
assert fingerprint("45\n", 0) == f1 != fingerprint("46\n", 0)
